title: Resisting GenAI in Education.
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin, a parent, educator and screen-time consultant, argues that schools should refuse generative AI tools, especially for children. She opens with district decisions she witnessed, from GenAI on school-issued devices to a recommendation that an overloaded teacher use AI to grade essays, and asks why technology companies get a say in how teachers teach. Drawing on Benjamin Riley, she explains GenAI as prediction rather than thinking, which makes it a cognitive forklift that displaces the very mental effort education exists to produce. Her case adds child brain development, the slippery slope of AI tutors and buddies, the failure of earlier ed-tech promises and the social cost of personalised learning. She closes with questions parents can put to administrators and a call for mass refusal until evidence and purpose are clear.
points: GenAI predicts likely text rather than thinking, so its confident errors are no different in kind from its correct answers, which is a particular hazard for young children.
Because education is about engaging students in a cognitive process and GenAI displaces that process, the author treats it as a cognitive forklift in the gym of learning.
Telling students to use AI responsibly ignores that their executive function is undeveloped and the temptation to outsource homework is strong.
Personalised learning through GenAI isolates students from the communal struggle and teacher relationships through which they become thinking adults.
The piece offers practical questions for administrators (what problem is being solved, what evidence supports it, can we opt out) and urges parent refusal as the quickest lever for change.
quotes: However, what Generative AI can do is very, very different from what you and I do when we are thinking. When humans think, we don’t scan past knowledge to predict what thoughts will come next. We use context, previous experiences, feelings, abstract thoughts to come up with ideas and new thoughts.
The goal of education is to engage students in a cognitive process. GenerativeAI displaces the cognitive process– it does the “thinking” for students.
Students will use it to do their homework, write their essays, and cheat on their tests. Telling them to “use it responsibly” is irresponsible and completely misunderstands brain development.
We cannot keep attempting to solve every problem with technology. GenAI is a hammer in search of a nail. What problem is it really attempting to solve?

Learning happens in a communal environment, with other people and in the context of relationships to teachers. GenAI and “personalizing instruction” siphons students into individual silos of thinking and prevents the cognitive conflicts and social struggles necessary to become thinking adults.

So today, until things change, we have to fight back by refusing to allow our children to participate in any Generative AI tools in school. If enough parents say “No,” then schools will be forced to look again.
